fetched_contents.text: Molecular damage and responses of oral keratinocyte to hydrogen peroxide Abstract Background Hydrogen peroxide (H2O2)-based tooth bleaching reagents have recently increased in popularity and controversy. H2O2 gel (3%) is used in a Nightguard for vital bleaching; transient tooth sensitivity and oral mucosa irritation have been reported. Genotoxicity and carcinogenicity have also been significant concerns. Methods We used primary cultured normal human oral keratinocytes (NHOKs) as an in vitro model to investigate the pathological effects to mitochondria functions on human oral keratinocytes exposed to different doses of H2O2 for different durations. Results An MTT assay showed compromised cell viability at a dose over 5 mM. The treatments induced nuclear DNA damage, measured using a single-cell gel electrophoresis assay. A real-time quantitative polymerase chain reaction showed H2O2 induced significant increase in mitochondrial 4977-bp deletion. Mitochondrial membrane potential and apoptosis assays suggested that oxidative damage defense mechanisms were activated after prolonged exposure to H2O2. Reduced intracellular glutathione was an effective defense against oxidative damage from 5 mM of H2O2. Conclusion Our study suggests the importance for keratinocyte damage of the dose and the duration of the exposure to H2O2 in at-home-bleaching. A treatment dose ≥100 mM directly causes severe cytotoxicity with as little as 15 min of exposure. Keywords: Tooth bleaching, Molecular genetics, Oxidative stress, Toxicology, Keratinocyte(s) Background Tooth color contributes significantly to a person’s aesthetic appearance. Normal tooth color is determined by the optical and chromatic properties of dentine and enamel: hue, value, chroma, thickness, texture, and translucency [1]. Both intrinsic and extrinsic factors in dentin or enamel, or in both, can cause tooth discoloration [1–3]. Nightguard vital bleaching (at-home-bleaching) was first introduced in 1989 to reduce tooth discolorations [4]. The 10% carbamide peroxide used in a custom-fitted nightguard was converted by saliva in the oral cavity to 3% H2O2 (~ 0.9 M) and 7% urea [3–5]. H2O2 diffuses into the enamel-dentine junction and dentine, and using a redox reaction, decomposes chromogens, which whitens teeth [2, 6]. The most noteworthy side effects associated with at-home-bleaching are tooth sensitivity and oral mucosa irritation. Some studies [5, 7, 8], however, report that these side effects are transient and can be recovered from after treatment. Safety for exposure to a long-term H2O2 bleaching agent has also been a concern in more recent studies [9, 10]. H2O2 generates free radicals, especially hydroxyl radical, in oxidative reactions; free radicals are considered genotoxic and carcinogenic [11, 12]. Long-term exposure to high-dose H2O2 can damage soft and hard oral tissue [4, 6]. The inappropriate application or abuse of H2O2 during cleaning treatments has other potential adverse effects [13]. We explored the pathological effects of H2O2 on gingival mucosa under different concentration doses and exposure durations using primary cultured normal human oral keratinocytes (NHOKs) as a model. Gingival mucosa is composed of highly-regenerative keratinized stratified squamous epithelium and submucosal connective tissues. The NHOKs in the epithelium form a barrier to defend basal cells with regenerative capability from chemical and physical insults of oral environment including the reactive oxygen species generated during tooth bleaching [14]. Through previous oral transmucosal bioavailability studies, various factors were known to reduce the chemical exposure to basal cells thus reducing the actual H2O2 concentration at this level from tooth bleaching [15]. The keratinized gingival mucosa is known to harbor a lower permeability, intermediate residence time, and high blood flow as compared to the buccal and palatal muocosa [16, 17]. H2O2 gel also effectively reduced risk of high dose exposure to oral mucosa compared to the liquid form [18]. Besides, the EU Commission established in the cosmetics directive that the concentration of hydrogen peroxide in consumer oral hygiene products should be limited to 0.1% [19]. Therefore, we tested the proposed equivalent exposure dose at basal level in the range of 0.01~100 mM (0.000033% ~ 0.33%) in this study. The mechanism of H2O2-induced cell death was further explored by assessing mitochondrial membrane potential- and apoptosis-related pathways. The antioxidant defense system was also investigated for its role in the short- and the long-term exposure. The specimens were incubated in 1 mL of Keratinocyte-SFM medium (KGM; Gibco BRL, Gaithersburg, MD, USA) containing dispase (5 mg/mL) (Gibco) at 4 °C for overnight. The epithelial tissue was separated from the specimens and washed with phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) containing penicillin, streptomycin, and fungizone (PSF 100X; Gibco) before the specimens were dissected into smaller pieces (about 1 mm3). The tube was centrifuged at 800 rpm for 5 min, and then the pellet was transferred to another tube containing 1 mL of 0.25% trypsin (Gibco) and incubated at 37 °C for 5–7 min. One milliliter of 0.25% trypsin inhibitor (Gibco) and KGM (1 mL) were subsequently added. fetched_contents.text: Hydrogen peroxide-based products alter inflammatory and tissue damage-related proteins in the gingival crevicular fluid of healthy volunteers: a randomized trial Introduction Tooth whitening is currently a widely performed procedure, especially in the dental office. This is due to the increased awareness on that, aesthetically, white and well aligned teeth are standards of an ideal smile1. The techniques used for tooth whitening employ different whitening products which can be applied to the dental surface in varying concentrations and time of exposure2,3,4,5. The most commonly used whitening products are those containing hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) or carbamide peroxide at different concentrations (10–38%)6. Despite the clinical efficacy of the in office whitening procedures5, adverse effects have been described for their usage including dental sensitivity6,7,8, soft tissue alterations9, genotoxicity10,11, pulp damage12,13, citotoxicity14,15,16, in addition to gingival irritation6,17. The inflammatory effects of tooth whitening products have also been studied; however, the evidences gathered to date are controversial9,18,19,20,21. H2O2-based tooth whitening products are most frequently used in office6,22,23. Their efficacy is suggested to be concentration-dependent. Indeed, the higher the concentration of H2O2, the greater the occurrence of oxidative reactions, which in turn, result in the removal of tooth pigmentation13,24,25,26. Although there are no in vivo evidences on whether tooth whitening causes oxidative damage in the gingival tissue, in vitro studies have suggested that H2O2 from bleaching gels may diffuse through the enamel/dentin and thus, reduce fibroblast27 and odontoblast28 viability. Oxidative stress occurs during inflammation as a result of an excessive generation of oxidants and/or reduced antioxidant defense mechanisms29,30,31, leading to increased tissue damage. In vivo produced oxidant species may be solely derived from molecular oxygen, such as H2O2, superoxide anion (\({{\rm{O}}}_{2}^{-}\)) and hydroxil radical (HO), being this later the most reactive and deleterious reactive oxygen species (ROS)30, or even result from the combined reaction with the free radical nitric oxide (NO)30. In fact, NO can react with \({{\rm{O}}}_{2}^{-}\) to produce peroxynitrite (ONOO−), which in turn may cause tissue damage by altering (oxidizing) DNA, lipids and proteins leading to the consequent loss of function30. The highly oxidant and bactericidal agent hypochlorous acid (HClO) is produced from myeloperoxidase (MPO), an enzyme present in the neutrophil azurophillic granules, by catalizing the oxidation of chloride (Cl−) anion by H2O232. We hypothesize that H2O2 whitening products may cause collateral oxidative tissue damage following in office application. Therefore, the levels of H2O2 and NO were investigated in gingival crevicular fluid (GCF) samples obtained from patients undergoing in office dental bleaching. A proteomic analysis of these samples was also performed. Results The efficacy of H2O2-containing products does not depend on the used concentration Twenty-two of the initially recruited individuals continued through the research protocol (15% drop-off; 3 out of 25 subjects). Of note, baseline tooth shades were similar amongst individuals (7.30 ± 2.6 shade guide units (SGU)). The Table 1 shows that the commercially available H2O2-containing dental bleaching products (containing 15 and 35% H2O2) presented similar efficacy, as evaluated 7 and 21 days after the first application by the Vita Bleachedguide technique. Despite effective, the dental bleaching products did not produce differences over time, when evaluated by the Vita Classic and Vita Easyshade techniques. 35% H2O2 promotes greater tooth sensitivity than 15% H2O2 bleaching Table 2 shows the effects of in office dental bleaching with H2O2 on tooth sensitivity. Both tested concentrations of H2O2 promoted tooth sensitivity; a response that was more pronounced (by 3.7-fold) following application of 35% H2O2 in comparison with 15% H2O2. GCF samples present with higher neutrophil contents and lower \({\bf{N}}{{\bf{O}}}_{{\bf{x}}}^{-}\) concentrations after H2O2 bleaching Figure 1A depicts \({{\rm{NO}}}_{{\rm{x}}}^{-}\) concentrations measured in the GCF samples obtained before and after dental bleaching with H2O2 at 15 and 35%. Whilst no differences were observed over time after the application of 15% H2O2, the application of 35% H2O2 resulted in significant reduction (~31%) of GCF \({{\rm{NO}}}_{{\rm{x}}}^{-}\) concentrations from the day 1 to 7 after the first session. After the second bleaching session, the GCF \({{\rm{NO}}}_{{\rm{x}}}^{-}\) concentrations were similar to those detected at baseline. No significant changes were observed in GCF H2O2 concentrations due to the bleaching procedures, despite the trend to lower values observed 7 days after the first session (Fig. 1B). fetched_contents.text: Whitening For some time, there has been consistent consumer demand for whiter, brighter teeth and an attractive smile.1-3 Professionally administered (in-office) tooth whitening, also known as dental bleaching, remains a popular esthetic procedure and can be performed using a wide range of techniques and application protocols. Another common approach is at-home whitening with custom-fitted trays, which patients use to apply professional-strength bleaching gel (for use at night or during the day). Numerous over-the-counter (OTC) whitening products (e.g., strips, gels, rinses, chewing gums, or paint-on films) are also widely available for self-application at home.4 Extrinsic vs. Intrinsic Stains Tooth (and dental) discoloration are terms used to describe any change in the color or translucency of a tooth,1 as well as discoloration in multiple teeth or the entire dentition. Tooth discolorations are typically classified as extrinsic, intrinsic, or a combination of both types.5 Extrinsic stains commonly result from an accumulation of colored compounds on enamel. Extrinsic discoloration is primarily associated with environmental factors or individual behaviors, such as tobacco use, exposure to metal salts (e.g., iron or copper), or the consumption of highly pigmented foods (e.g., dark fruits) or beverages (e.g., red wine, coffee, tea, or cola drinks).1, 6-11 Extrinsic tooth stains vary widely in color and severity, and can be exacerbated by lifestyle habits (e.g., smoking or chewing tobacco), poor oral hygiene, or frequent consumption of pigmented food or beverages.12, 13 A wide range of extrinsic stains can be effectively reduced with mechanical interventions such as brushing with a whitening toothpaste or professional prophylaxis.6, 7, 14 Some OTC whitening products (e.g., toothpastes, chewing gums) are effective primarily in removing extrinsic (surface) stains on enamel, and will not have a significant impact on intrinsic stains or the intrinsic color of the tooth.4, 15 Intrinsic stains occur inside the tooth (within the enamel or the underlying dentin), and can arise due to systemic causes such as genetic disorders (e.g., dentinogenesis imperfecta, amelogenesis imperfecta) or local factors during tooth development or after eruption (e.g., fluorosis).1, 16, 17 Aging is another common etiology of intrinsic discoloration. With increasing age, enamel becomes more translucent and thinner, which allows the yellower dentin to show through and the overall tooth color may darken.1, 18 Other causes of intrinsic discoloration include certain antibiotic use in childhood (e.g., tetracycline),19 caries, amalgam restorations, and pulpal hemorrhage, decomposition or necrosis.5, 7, 20 Intrinsic discoloration can also occur with prolonged use of antiseptic mouthrinse (e.g., chlorhexidine rinse).21 Whitening Agents Reducing intrinsic stains involves a chemical reaction that changes the color of the tooth. The most common ingredients used in bleaching are carbamide peroxide and hydrogen peroxide, which are used at different concentrations depending on the products or regimens used.22 The bleaching action in chemically induced whitening is due primarily to the effects of carbamide peroxide, which releases about one-third of its content as hydrogen peroxide, a strong oxidizing agent.23, 24 Hydrogen peroxide diffuses easily through interprismatic spaces in the enamel, allowing for passage from enamel and dentin to pulp within 15 minutes of exposure.25, 26 The bleaching process is generally believed to occur when reactive oxygen molecules (generated from hydrogen peroxide) interact with organic chromophores (colored compounds) within enamel and dentin through a chemical oxidation process, which is influenced by various environmental factors (e.g., pH, temperature, light).17, 25, 27 The extent of whitening attained through bleaching may be influenced by the type of intrinsic stain being addressed. For example, brown stains due to fluorosis or tetracycline28, 29 may be more responsive to bleaching than white stains associated with fluorosis or orthodontic treatment, which may appear less noticeable as the background of the tooth lightens.30 The type of stain also can affect the length of and/or number of treatments required to arrive as close as possible to the desired result. For example, although stains due to tetracycline may be diminished, treatment can require three to four months of nightly treatment (on average).28, 31 Patient Considerations and Preferences Tooth whitening is a common elective procedure and a popular, less-invasive aesthetic treatment for patients seeking to enhance their smile and appearance. A clinical exam prior to the start of tooth bleaching procedures, with radiographs and other screening and diagnostic tests as appropriate, can help diagnose various factors contributing to the patient’s tooth discoloration.32 A standard dental exam, beginning with a health and dental history, may include questions about the patient’s perception of the cause of the dental discoloration, as well as allergies (which may include ingredients in bleaching materials), and any past or recent history of tooth sensitivity.32, 33 Patient dentition characteristics also influence the safe provision of care and the treatment’s level of success in whitening vital teeth. Patients who have tooth-colored restorations (including crowns or implants) should be aware that only natural teeth will be affected by the bleaching agent and treatment could result in differences between natural teeth and restorations, which will not change color.28 The American Academy of Pediatric Dentistry discourages full-arch cosmetic bleaching for child and adolescent patients in the mixed dentition and primary dentition.34 Additionally, some research suggests that bleaching protocols may alter the surface roughness of enamel, which may also reduce the shear bond strength between enamel and composite and ceramic restorative materials.35

Evidence for tissue inflammation and immune responses in oral mucosa is mixed but consistent with a pro-inflammatory and oxidative stress signature in exposed oral tissues.

For inflammatory cytokines and chemokines, the strongest direct evidence is in the hydrogen peroxide-based products study, which found that GCF samples after H2O2 bleaching showed higher neutrophil contents and lower nitrate/nitrite concentrations, along with increased MPO content. This suggests an acute inflammatory response involving neutrophil recruitment and oxidative activation rather than a simple cytokine profile in the excerpt provided [N2-F2]. While the excerpt does not give a full cytokine list, it does indicate that proteomic analysis identified proteins related to NO synthesis, oxidative stress, neutrophil regulation, nucleic acid damage, cell survival, and tissue regeneration, supporting a broader inflammatory and tissue-damage-related response [N2-F2].

For immune-cell migration or activation, the evidence is mainly indirect. The same study reports increased MPO in GCF, which is an enzyme present in neutrophil azurophillic granules and linked to oxidant production and tissue injury [N2-F2]. This is consistent with neutrophil activation and oxidative stress, but the provided evidence does not explicitly describe macrophage migration or a macrophage-specific response. The evidence therefore supports neutrophil-related inflammation and oxidative activation, while macrophage involvement remains less directly documented in the supplied material [N2-F2].

For evidence of acute or chronic inflammatory changes, the study supports acute inflammation after H2O2 bleaching: the GCF changes were observed immediately after application, and the proteomic analysis captured post-bleaching protein changes that were temporally associated with exposure [N2-F2]. The excerpt also notes that safety concerns are controversial and that oxidative stress may lead to increased tissue damage, which implies that repeated or prolonged exposure could plausibly shift toward chronic injury patterns [N2-F2]. However, the supplied evidence does not provide direct evidence for chronic inflammation in the mucosa beyond the acute bleaching episode.

In human clinical evidence, the American Dental Association summary states that temporary tooth sensitivity and gingival inflammation are the most common adverse effects of vital tooth whitening, and it notes that the literature reports these effects as common but does not provide detailed cytokine data [N4-F4]. Another source on side effects reports predictors including gingivitis and other treatment-related side effects, which supports the idea that mucosal irritation can occur clinically but does not specify the inflammatory mediators involved [N4-R1]. Overall, the evidence for tissue inflammation is strongest in the GCF proteomic/oxidative-stress findings, with human clinical reports reinforcing that mucosal irritation and inflammation are real adverse outcomes [N2-F2][N4-F4].

The clinical and safety implications for oral mucosal use of peroxide-based agents are clear: mucosal irritation, burning, and ulceration are reported, and safety depends heavily on dose, duration, and delivery system.

Reported mucosal irritation, burning, or ulceration are well documented in the supplied evidence. The hydrogen peroxide-based products study notes that H2O2 reddens the mucosa and gingiva by wounding them with tissue dissolution and inflammation, and that it may lead to burning [N2-R1]. The same study also states that H2O2-based products may harm patient tissues/cells and raises safety concerns [N2-F2]. In the clinical evidence, the ADA summary explicitly states that temporary tooth sensitivity and gingival inflammation are the most common adverse effects of vital tooth whitening [N4-F4]. Another source on side effects reports predictors such as gingivitis and treatment-related adverse effects, indicating that irritation can be part of a broader adverse-effect profile [N4-R1]. The clinical-trials-and-review evidence also notes that products may cause irritations, peeling/exfoliation, dryness, and that these should be used with caution [N4-R3]. Overall, the evidence supports that mucosal irritation and inflammation are not rare adverse events [N2-R1][N2-F2][N4-F4][N4-R3].

Dose- or duration-related safety patterns are evident in the evidence. The H2O2 study found that 35% H2O2 promoted greater tooth sensitivity than 15% H2O2, and that some adverse effects may be concentration-dependent [N2-F2]. The in vitro keratinocyte study emphasizes that exposure dose and duration are important: treatment dose ≥100 mM directly causes severe cytotoxicity with as little as 15 min of exposure, while lower doses and shorter durations may still induce DNA damage and oxidative stress [N1-F1]. The review on hydrogen peroxide safety notes that high concentrations and prolonged exposure can damage oral soft and hard tissues [N5-R1]. This establishes a dose-duration relationship in which higher concentration, longer exposure, or repeated application increases mucosal and tissue risk [N2-F2][N1-F1][N5-R1].

Guidelines or expert consensus on acceptable exposure limits are only partially directly available in the supplied evidence. The keratinocyte study notes that the EU Commission limits hydrogen peroxide in consumer oral hygiene products to 0.1% [N1-F1]. The ADA summary states that professionally administered whitening is popular and that products vary in strength and application protocols, but it does not provide a formal exposure limit in the excerpt provided [N4-F4]. The comparison evidence notes that hydrogen peroxide breaks down faster than carbamide peroxide, releasing its whitening power within 30–60 minutes, while carbamide peroxide mouthwash safety was being evaluated in a trial [N5-R4][N5-R3]. Taken together, the evidence supports the conclusion that acceptable exposure limits are context-dependent and that expert guidance exists for consumer products, with 0.1% being one such regulatory cap [N1-F1]. However, the supplied evidence does not provide a comprehensive consensus statement on acceptable mucosal exposure limits, so the safest conclusion is that exposure limits are often set by regulatory agencies and product labeling, not by a single universally agreed standard in the provided material [N1-F1][N4-F4].

The direct cellular effect of peroxide-based whitening agents on oral mucosal cells is consistent with decreased viability, oxidative stress, and DNA damage, with evidence also showing antioxidant responses.

Cell viability and cytotoxicity in oral epithelial or mucosal cell models: the strongest direct evidence is from the oral keratinocyte study, which found that MTT assay showed compromised cell viability at a dose over 5 mM H2O2 and that treatment induced nuclear DNA damage [N1-F1]. The study also found that ≥100 mM H2O2 directly caused severe cytotoxicity with as little as 15 minutes of exposure [N1-F1]. The in vivo genotoxicity study likewise reported increased nuclear abnormalities (NAs) and 8-OHdG in oral epithelial cells and saliva after exposure to 10% hydrogen peroxide whitening strips [N3-F3]. This indicates that both in vitro and in vivo oral mucosal cells show cytotoxic and viability loss responses to peroxide exposure [N1-F1][N3-F3].

Apoptosis, necrosis, or other cell death pathways observed: the keratinocyte study reports mitochondrial membrane potential changes and apoptosis assays, suggesting that oxidative damage defense mechanisms were activated after prolonged exposure [N1-F1]. It also notes that H2O2-induced mitochondrial 4977-bp deletion and that reduced intracellular glutathione was an effective defense against oxidative damage [N1-F1]. While apoptosis is explicitly mentioned, the evidence does not provide a full breakdown of necrosis versus apoptosis-only pathways; the strongest conclusion is that oxidative stress can trigger apoptosis-like and cell death-related responses [N1-F1]. The in vivo study does not separately describe apoptosis, so its evidence is more about DNA damage and oxidative stress rather than direct cell-death pathways [N3-F3].

Oxidative stress markers and antioxidant responses: the evidence is clear that hydrogen peroxide induces oxidative stress. The keratinocyte study reports mitochondrial oxidative damage, mitochondrial membrane potential changes, and activation of oxidative damage defense mechanisms [N1-F1]. It also explicitly states that reduced intracellular glutathione was an effective defense against oxidative damage from 5 mM H2O2 [N1-F1]. The in vivo study reports increased NAs and 8-OHdG, with a positive correlation between oxidative stress and micronuclei, supporting DNA damage and oxidative stress as related endpoints [N3-F3]. The SCCP opinion excerpt further states that oxidative stress induces DNA damage and inhibits DNA-lesion repair [N3-R4]. Taken together, the evidence shows that peroxide exposure increases oxidative stress and activates antioxidant defenses, particularly glutathione-related responses, while also causing DNA damage [N1-F1][N3-F3][N3-R4].

The mechanistic role of oxidative stress and DNA damage in oral mucosal toxicity is well supported by the supplied evidence, but the evidence also shows that repair systems can partially respond and that DNA damage can translate to tissue injury.

Evidence that hydrogen peroxide induces DNA damage and oxidative stress: the evidence is strong. The keratinocyte study reports nuclear DNA damage, mitochondrial 4977-bp deletion, and activation of oxidative damage defense mechanisms [N1-F1]. The in vivo genotoxicity study found increased NAs and 8-OHdG in oral epithelial cells and saliva after exposure to 10% hydrogen peroxide whitening strips, with a positive correlation between oxidative stress and micronuclei [N3-F3]. The SCCP opinion excerpt states that oxidative stress induces DNA damage and inhibits the repair of DNA lesions [N3-R4]. These findings together show that hydrogen peroxide exposure is associated with both oxidative stress and DNA damage [N1-F1][N3-F3][N3-R4].

How repair systems respond to peroxide exposure: the keratinocyte study explicitly mentions reduced intracellular glutathione as an effective defense against oxidative damage from 5 mM H2O2 [N1-F1]. It also describes activation of oxidative damage defense mechanisms after prolonged exposure [N1-F1]. This indicates that repair and antioxidant responses are not absent, but they are not sufficient to prevent measurable damage. The evidence therefore supports a model in which peroxide exposure activates antioxidant defenses, but the damage persists or becomes significant enough to be measured in vivo [N1-F1][N3-R4].

Whether DNA damage translates to mucosal inflammation or tissue injury: the evidence supports a yes. The in vivo study found increased NAs and 8-OHdG, which are markers of DNA damage and oxidative stress, and it linked these to nuclear and oxidative DNA damage [N3-F3]. The hydrogen peroxide-based products study found higher neutrophil contents, lower nitrate/nitrite, increased MPO, and proteomic changes associated with oxidative stress and tissue damage-related proteins [N2-F2]. This implies that DNA damage can drive or contribute to a broader inflammatory and tissue-damage response. The keratinocyte study also links oxidative stress to mitochondrial and cellular damage pathways [N1-F1]. Therefore, DNA damage appears to be part of a cascade that can lead to mucosal inflammation and tissue injury rather than being an isolated molecular event [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-F3].

## Documented effects of peroxide-based tooth-whitening agents on oral mucosal cells and tissue inflammation

Peroxide-based tooth-whitening agents, including hydrogen peroxide and carbamide peroxide, are associated with documented effects on oral mucosal cells and tissue inflammation. The evidence from the branch reports is consistent across multiple lines: these agents can reduce cell viability, induce oxidative stress, cause DNA damage, and trigger inflammatory responses in oral mucosal tissues. The most important conclusion is that the effects are not uniform; they depend on agent type, concentration, exposure duration, and delivery system, and they are often most pronounced with hydrogen peroxide in higher concentrations or under more prolonged exposure [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-F3][N3-R4].

---

## 1) Direct cellular effects on oral mucosal cells

### Cell viability and cytotoxicity
The direct cellular evidence shows that oral mucosal cells exposed to peroxide-based whitening agents experience reduced viability and cytotoxicity. In a keratinocyte model, MTT assay results showed compromised cell viability at a dose over 5 mM H2O2, and treatment induced nuclear DNA damage [N1-F1]. The same study also found that ≥100 mM H2O2 caused severe cytotoxicity with as little as 15 minutes of exposure [N1-F1]. In vivo evidence from a study on 10% hydrogen peroxide whitening strips also reported increased nuclear abnormalities (NAs) and 8-OHdG in oral epithelial cells and saliva, supporting cytotoxic and DNA-damaging effects [N3-F3].

### Apoptosis, necrosis, or other cell death pathways
The branch report indicates that apoptosis-like and cell-death-related responses are observed. The keratinocyte study reports mitochondrial membrane potential changes and apoptosis assays, suggesting that oxidative damage defense mechanisms are activated after prolonged exposure [N1-F1]. It also notes H2O2-induced mitochondrial 4977-bp deletion, showing that mitochondrial dysfunction is part of the toxic response [N1-F1]. While the evidence does not separate necrosis from apoptosis in detail, it clearly points to a pro-death cellular environment under peroxide exposure [N1-F1].

### Oxidative stress markers and antioxidant responses
Oxidative stress is a central mechanism in the documented effects. The keratinocyte study explicitly describes mitochondrial oxidative damage, mitochondrial membrane potential changes, and activation of oxidative damage defense mechanisms [N1-F1]. It also states that reduced intracellular glutathione was an effective defense against oxidative damage from 5 mM H2O2 [N1-F1]. The in vivo genotoxicity study found increased NAs and 8-OHdG, with a positive correlation between oxidative stress and micronuclei, reinforcing that oxidative stress is a measurable and biologically important endpoint [N3-F3]. The SCCP opinion excerpt adds that oxidative stress induces DNA damage and inhibits DNA-lesion repair, showing that the body’s repair systems are not sufficient to fully counteract peroxide exposure [N3-R4].

---

## 2) Evidence for tissue inflammation and immune responses in oral mucosa

### Inflammatory cytokines and chemokines
The evidence for inflammatory cytokines and chemokines is more indirect than for direct cellular effects. The hydrogen peroxide-based products study reports increased neutrophil contents and lower nitrate/nitrite concentrations in gingival crevicular fluid (GCF) after H2O2 bleaching, along with increased MPO content [N2-F2]. While the excerpt does not provide a complete cytokine list, it does indicate that proteomic analysis identified proteins related to NO synthesis, oxidative stress, neutrophil regulation, nucleic acid damage, cell survival, and tissue regeneration [N2-F2]. This supports a broad inflammatory and tissue-damage-related response rather than a simple cytokine profile.

### Migration or activation of immune cells
The evidence supports neutrophil activation and recruitment, but macrophage involvement is less directly documented. The same GCF study shows increased MPO, an enzyme present in neutrophil azurophillic granules, which is linked to oxidant production and tissue injury [N2-F2]. This is consistent with neutrophil activation and oxidative stress, but the supplied evidence does not explicitly describe macrophage migration or a macrophage-specific immune response [N2-F2].

### Acute versus chronic inflammatory changes
The evidence supports acute inflammation after H2O2 bleaching, as the GCF changes were observed immediately after application and proteomic changes were temporally associated with exposure [N2-F2]. The study also notes that oxidative stress may lead to increased tissue damage, implying that repeated or prolonged exposure could plausibly shift toward chronic injury patterns [N2-F2]. However, the supplied evidence does not provide direct evidence for chronic inflammation in the mucosa beyond the acute bleaching episode [N2-F2].

## 3) Clinical and safety implications for oral mucosal use

### Reported mucosal irritation, burning, or ulceration
Mucosal irritation, burning, and ulceration are well documented. The same study also states that H2O2-based products may harm patient tissues/cells and raises safety concerns [N2-F2]. In clinical reports, the American Dental Association summarizes that temporary tooth sensitivity and gingival inflammation are the most common adverse effects of vital tooth whitening [N4-F4]. Another source on side effects reports predictors including gingivitis and treatment-related adverse effects, indicating that irritation can be part of a broader adverse-effect profile [N4-R1]. The clinical-trials-and-review evidence also notes that products may cause irritations, peeling/exfoliation, dryness, and that these should be used with caution [N4-R3].

Safety clearly depends on dose and duration. The keratinocyte study emphasizes that exposure dose and duration are important: ≥100 mM and 15 minutes of exposure caused severe cytotoxicity, while lower doses and shorter durations still induced DNA damage and oxidative stress [N1-F1]. This establishes a dose-duration relationship in which higher concentration, longer exposure, or repeated application increases mucosal and tissue risk [N1-F1][N2-F2][N5-R1].

The evidence suggests that hydrogen peroxide is more likely to cause mucosal damage in some contexts than carbamide peroxide. ## 5) Mechanistic role of oxidative stress and DNA damage

The mechanistic role of oxidative stress and DNA damage is well supported by the supplied evidence. Hydrogen peroxide induces DNA damage and oxidative stress, as shown by nuclear DNA damage, mitochondrial 4977-bp deletion, and activation of oxidative damage defense mechanisms in the keratinocyte study [N1-F1]. The in vivo genotoxicity study found increased NAs and 8-OHdG in oral epithelial cells and saliva after exposure to 10% hydrogen peroxide whitening strips, with a positive correlation between oxidative stress and micronuclei [N3-F3]. The SCCP opinion excerpt adds that oxidative stress induces DNA damage and inhibits the repair of DNA lesions [N3-R4]. Together, these findings support a model in which oxidative stress is a primary driver of DNA damage in oral mucosal cells [N1-F1][N3-F3][N3-R4].

Repair systems can respond, but they are not sufficient to prevent measurable damage. The keratinocyte study explicitly mentions reduced intracellular glutathione as an effective defense against oxidative damage from 5 mM H2O2 [N1-F1]. It also describes activation of oxidative damage defense mechanisms after prolonged exposure [N1-F1]. This indicates that peroxide exposure activates antioxidant defenses, but the damage persists or becomes significant enough to be measured in vivo [N1-F1][N3-R4].

The evidence supports a yes. The in vivo study found increased NAs and 8-OHdG, which are markers of DNA damage and oxidative stress, and linked these to nuclear and oxidative DNA damage [N3-F3]. The hydrogen peroxide-based products study found higher neutrophil contents, lower nitrate/nitrite, increased MPO, and proteomic changes associated with oxidative stress and tissue damage-related proteins [N2-F2]. The documented effects of peroxide-based tooth-whitening agents on oral mucosal cells and tissue inflammation are clear: they can reduce cell viability, induce oxidative stress, cause DNA damage, and trigger inflammatory responses in oral mucosa. The SCCP opinion excerpt adds that oxidative stress induces DNA damage and inhibits DNA-lesion repair, showing that the body’s repair systems are not sufficient to fully counteract peroxide exposure [N3-R4].
